qs.q: What is the characteristic hormonal profile found in Turner syndrome due to gonadal dysgenesis?
o: Low follicle-stimulating hormone, low luteinizing hormone, low oestrogen
Normal gonadotropin levels with low oestrogen and normal feedback
High prolactin with suppressed gonadotropins and normal oestrogen
High follicle-stimulating hormone, high luteinizing hormone, low oestrogen
qs.e: Turner syndrome features streak gonads causing primary ovarian failure, which yields very high gonadotropins due to a lack of negative feedback, alongside low oestrogen. This hypergonadotropic hypogonadism results in primary amenorrhea.

qs.q: An infant with Turner syndrome is found to have a large, soft, translucent mass in the left neck. Histologic examination reveals dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelium. What is the standard designation for this anomaly?
qs.e: Cystic hygromas are cavernous lymphangiomas typically found in the head and neck region of children, frequently associated with Turner syndrome. Simple lymphangiomas and hemangiomas lack these large, macroscopic cystic spaces.

qs.q: Which of the following interventions is specifically indicated for the management of children with growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, or chronic kidney disease who fail to catch up in height?
o: Therapeutic F-75 milk formulas given indefinitely
Daily growth hormone replacement therapy injections
qs.e: Growth hormone therapy via daily injection is used for growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic kidney disease, Prader-Willi syndrome, and short children born small for gestational age. Corticosteroids can actually suppress growth rather than treat these conditions.

qs.q: A newborn presents with a congenital heart defect associated with Turner syndrome. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Turner syndrome is classically associated with coarctation of the aorta and a bicuspid aortic valve. Atrioventricular septal defect is more commonly linked with Trisomy 21.

qs.q: NOT a clinical feature of Turner syndrome?
qs.e: Turner syndrome affects females (45,X) — there are no testes. The correct gonadal finding is streak ovaries.

o: Normal follicle-stimulating hormone, normal luteinizing hormone, low oestrogen

qs.e: Turner syndrome is associated with streak gonads, resulting in primary ovarian failure. This leads to very high FSH and LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) and low oestrogen, causing primary amenorrhea.

qs.q: Turner syndrome (45,X0) shows which hormonal pattern?
o: High FSH, high LH, low oestrogen
Low FSH, low LH, low oestrogen
qs.e: Turner syndrome: streak gonads → primary ovarian failure → very high FSH and LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism), low oestrogen, primary amenorrhoea. Short stature, webbed neck, bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of aorta.

qs.q: Turner syndrome (45,X) causes infertility because of
o: Premature ovarian failure — streak gonads → primary amenorrhea + elevated FSH/LH
qs.e: Turner syndrome: 45,X (or mosaic). Streak gonads (fibrous tissue replacing ovaries) → no estrogen/progesterone → no negative feedback → elevated FSH and LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism). Features: short stature, webbed neck, shield chest, coarctation of aorta, horseshoe kidney. Requires estrogen replacement for puberty induction and bone protection.

ai.title: Turner Syndrome
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Turner syndrome is a chromosomal disorder (45,X or variants) causing short stature, gonadal dysgenesis and multisystem anomalies. Diagnosis relies on karyotype; management is multidisciplinary, focusing on hormone replacement, cardiac surveillance and psychosocial support.

sections.p: Turner syndrome is a sex chromosome aneuploidy in phenotypic females, most commonly 45,X. Diagnosis is confirmed by karyotype or chromosomal microarray.
b: Full monosomy 45,X accounts for ~50% of cases; the rest are mosaics or structural abnormalities.
Diagnosis can be made prenatally (chorionic villus sampling, amniocentesis) or postnatally when clinical clues appear.

t.b: Confirms the presence of 45,X or mosaicism; a normal result excludes Turner syndrome.

sections.p: Severity is gauged by the extent of chromosomal loss and organ involvement, not by a formal stage system.
b: Mosaicism often yields milder phenotype (better growth, later puberty).
Full monosomy carries higher risk of cardiac, renal and endocrine complications.

sections.p: The primary cause is nondisjunction during meiosis I or II, producing a gamete lacking a second sex chromosome.
b: Maternal age >35 modestly increases risk of nondisjunction.
Environmental factors (e.g., radiation) have no proven link.

sections.p: Typical features appear in infancy or early childhood and include short stature, webbed neck, low posterior hairline, shield chest, and streak ovaries.
b: Growth failure: height <5th percentile despite normal nutrition.
Primary amenorrhea and lack of secondary sexual characteristics after age 13.
Cardiac: systolic murmur from bicuspid aortic valve or coarctation.
Renal anomalies (horseshoe kidney) in ~30%.

sections.p: Targeted tests evaluate the multisystem impact and guide management.

t.b: Detects bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, or aortic root dilation; abnormal findings require cardiology referral.
Screens for structural anomalies; normal scan reduces risk of urinary obstruction.
Identifies autoimmune thyroid disease; elevated TSH with low free T4 indicates hypothyroidism.
If radiography unavailable, use serial height measurements and growth charts.
Evaluates cardiovascular risk; dyslipidemia may need statin therapy later.

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening if missed.
b: Severe coarctation causing hypertension proximal to the lesion.
Aortic root dilation → dissection.
Undiagnosed hypothyroidism → growth failure, cognitive delay.
Autoimmune disorders (type 1 diabetes, celiac disease).

sections.p: Management is multidisciplinary, addressing hormone deficiency, cardiac lesions, and psychosocial needs.
b: Growth hormone (GH) from age 4–6 years to improve final height; start after cardiac lesions are stabilised.
Estrogen replacement at 12–14 years to induce secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone health.
Surgical repair of coarctation or valve replacement when indicated.
Thyroid hormone replacement for hypothyroidism; monitor TSH every 6–12 months.
Screen for celiac disease, type 1 diabetes and lipid abnormalities; treat per standard guidelines.
Annual blood pressure and cardiac imaging (echocardiogram every 2–3 years).
Thyroid function every year.
Bone density scan after estrogen therapy begins.
Psychological support and fertility counselling in adolescence.

sections.p: Conditions sharing short stature or neck webbing can mislead.
b: Noonan syndrome – also has webbed neck but males are affected and has normal chromosomes.
Russell‑Silver syndrome – intrauterine growth restriction, triangular face, but no gonadal dysgenesis.

sections.p: Certain investigations may appear normal despite underlying disease.
b: Mosaic Turner may have a normal karyotype in peripheral blood; consider skin fibroblast analysis if suspicion remains.
Mild coarctation can be missed on physical exam; always confirm with Doppler echo if blood pressure gradient is >20 mmHg between arms and legs.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypertension or chest pain suggesting aortic dissection.
Sudden loss of consciousness or stroke symptoms.

faq.q: Why is growth hormone therapy started before estrogen?
faq.a: GH maximises linear growth; estrogen accelerates epiphyseal closure, limiting height gain.

faq.q: Can a girl with Turner syndrome become pregnant?
faq.a: Spontaneous pregnancy is rare; assisted reproduction with donor oocytes is possible after cardiac clearance.
Most cases are de novo nondisjunction; recurrence risk is low, but parental karyotyping is advised.

exam: What cardiac investigations are mandatory before starting growth hormone and why? — Echocardiography to rule out coarctation or bicuspid valve, preventing GH‑induced hypertension complications.
A 14‑year‑old girl with short stature, webbed neck and delayed puberty presents. Which single test confirms the diagnosis? — Karyotype (or chromosomal microarray) demonstrating 45,X or mosaicism.
How does mosaicism modify prognosis compared with classic 45,X? — Milder phenotype, better growth, later puberty, lower incidence of severe cardiac lesions.
Explain why estrogen replacement is started after growth hormone therapy. — Early estrogen would close growth plates, reducing final height; GH first optimises stature.
A patient with Turner syndrome develops hypertension; what is the most likely cause and next step? — Coarctation of the aorta; obtain echocardiography and refer for surgical or catheter‑based repair.
Which autoimmune disease is most prevalent in Turner syndrome and how is it screened? — Autoimmune thyroid disease; screen with TSH and free T4 annually.
What counseling should be given regarding fertility? — Natural conception is unlikely; discuss assisted reproduction with donor oocytes after cardiac evaluation.
Why might a peripheral blood karyotype be normal in a suspected Turner patient? — Mosaicism limited to other tissues; consider fibroblast culture or repeat testing if clinical suspicion persists.
